title: A year without a smartphone
text: When my smartphone slipped out of my hands and landed screen-down on a station platform, I felt a flicker of panic that was out of proportion to the damage. The repair would cost nearly as much as a new device, and my first instinct was simply to buy another one. Instead, partly from stubbornness and partly from curiosity, I decided to try something that sounded ridiculous even as I said it: to live without a smartphone for a year, using only a basic phone that could call and send texts.

The first fortnight was harder than I had expected. I kept reaching into my pocket for something that was no longer there, like a person who has given up smoking and still pats his jacket for a lighter. Waiting for a bus, a minute that used to vanish into scrolling suddenly lasted for ever, and I did not know where to look. My sister, who is not given to exaggeration, said that I looked like a man whose umbrella had been taken away in the rain. I also discovered how much of my daily life had been outsourced: maps, timetables, even my sense of what time it was.

Little by little, however, the discomfort turned into something more interesting. I started to notice details in the street that had always been there: a faded shop sign, a man feeding pigeons, the way light fell across a building at five o'clock. I began to walk home instead of taking the tram, and discovered two bookshops and a tiny bakery that I had passed for years without seeing. Conversations with friends changed too. Because nobody could check facts or photographs under the table, we simply had to talk, and some of the longest evenings of my year consisted of nothing more than arguments about things that nobody could look up.

There were, of course, costs. I missed invitations that were sent only through group chats, and for a while I felt **out of the loop** whenever friends referred to a joke or a photograph I had not seen. Once I arrived at a café twenty minutes late because I had not received a message saying that the meeting had moved. A colleague sighed that my experiment was charming but inconvenient for everybody else, and I had to admit that she had a point.

Yet, strangely, the things I lost I missed less than the things I gained. I read eleven books, more than in the previous three years. I learnt to ask strangers for directions, and I remembered how pleasant it is to receive a real answer from a real person. I slept better, since there was nothing glowing next to my pillow. Perhaps the most important change was harder to describe: my attention, which had been chopped into tiny pieces, slowly began to join up again. I even wrote letters, three of them, and received one reply, which I still keep.

A year later, I did buy a new smartphone, and it would be dishonest to say that I have given it up. But I now keep it in another room at night, I switch off most notifications, and I try to leave it at home when I go for a walk. I do not think the experiment turned me into a better person. It did, however, remind me that a tool is only useful when I decide when to pick it up, and not when it decides for me.
